beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Adwait Changan, and this video is about why you cannot check your AI agent's work. Today we are going to learn what to do instead. Not because reading its output is hard, but because at any real volume there are not enough hours in the day, and the arithmetic is worse than most people expect.

three output lines land, ending on the twist

props.command: I cannot read every run my agent produces. So how do I know it is working?
output: Reading one run carefully takes about ninety seconds.
At a thousand runs a day that is twenty-five human hours.
Sampling feels like the answer. The arithmetic says otherwise.

beats.act: ACT 1 — THE HOURS DO NOT EXIST
beats.narration_text: Start with the thing nobody writes down. Reading one agent run properly, checking what it did and whether the answer holds, takes roughly ninety seconds. That number is the whole problem, because it does not shrink as your volume grows.

beats.act: ACT 1 — THE HOURS DO NOT EXIST
beats.narration_text: Multiply it out and the ceiling arrives fast. Ten runs a day is nothing. A hundred costs two and a half hours, which is already somebody's morning. A thousand costs twenty-five hours a day. There are twenty-four. The line crosses before you reach the volume anyone would call production.

beats.act: ACT 2 — SAMPLING IS NOT THE ANSWER
beats.narration_text: Here is a two percent failure rate, sampled at five percent. At a thousand runs a day, twenty of them fail. You look at one. Nineteen failures go out every single day with nobody having read them, and your sample came back clean, which is exactly what it would do.

the unseen column holds in terracotta

props.artifactTitle: evals.py — sampling 5% of a 2% failure rate
props.artifactHeading: What a clean sample is compatible with

beats.narration_text: The honest limit is that evals only catch what you thought to check. They will never find the failure you did not imagine, and that is the one that will hurt. Sampling is still worth doing, not as coverage, but as the thing that tells you which new check to write.

props.title: They Catch What You Thought Of
props.body: An eval never finds the failure you did not imagine. Sampling stays useful — not as coverage, but as the thing that tells you which check to write next.
props.sparkLine: Sample to learn, not to cover.

beats.narration_text: So, the verdict. Reading one agent run properly takes about ninety seconds, and that constant does not shrink, so a thousand runs a day costs twenty-five human hours and there are twenty-four. Sampling five percent of a two percent failure rate leaves nineteen failed runs a day that nobody sees, and a clean sample is exactly what that looks like. Sampling harder does not rescue it: fifty percent still misses ten a day and costs twelve hours, and the only sample that misses nothing is all of it. So the question changes from whether a human read the run to whether anything would have noticed it was wrong, because a check costs the same at ten runs and ten thousand. The limit is that evals only catch what you thought to check.

props.artifactHeading: You cannot read your way to confidence
artifactLines: Reviewing one run takes ~90 seconds, and that constant does not shrink with volume.
1000 runs a day costs 25 human hours. There are 24.
Sampling 5% of a 2% failure rate leaves 19 failures a day unseen — and the sample looks clean.
Sampling harder does not fix it. Only 100% misses nothing, which is the 25-hour day again.
Ask whether anything would have NOTICED, not whether anyone read it. Checks cost the same at any volume.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here is the prompt. Here is what my agent does. Give me four checks that could run on every single execution without a human reading the output, and for each one tell me what failure it would catch and what it would completely miss. Then tell me which failure none of them would catch. Run that on something you have built. The last answer is your next eval, and usually the one you least want to hear.

props.command: Here is what my agent does. Give me four checks that could run on every execution without a human reading the output. For each: what failure does it catch, and what does it completely miss? Then tell me which failure none of them would catch.
output: The 'what would it miss' column is the useful half of the answer.
The failure none of them catch is your next eval.
